strengths: Interesting empirical observation that time series of different sampling granularities exhibit distinct joint amplitude/phase-frequency distributions, motivating an explicit design choice rather than treating all data uniformly.

Unifying diverse generative tasks (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection) under a single architecture and a single GLM-inspired autoregressive blank-infilling pre-training objective, avoiding task-specific heads/architectures, is a reasonably appealing design goal.

Broad experimental coverage across three task families and many baselines (Transformer-based, MLP-based, LLM-enhanced, and foundation models), plus ablations isolating the frequency and granularity attention components and pre-training vs. no-pretraining comparisons.
Some qualitative visualizations (forecasting, imputation, anomaly score plots) support that the model behaves reasonably on real data.
weaknesses: Reported improvements over strong baselines (e.g., PatchTST) are frequently marginal or mixed rather than clearly dominant; by the paper's own account PatchTST achieves best/second-best in 29 of 50 forecasting settings versus GTM's 43, and many MSE/MAE differences are in the third decimal, raising doubts about the practical significance of the proposed mechanisms.

The core architectural novelty (five fixed learnable 'granularity' key vectors keyed to a hand-crafted day/hour/minute/second/millisecond quintuple) is ad hoc: it is unclear how this generalizes to arbitrary or unseen granularities, why five discrete slots are sufficient, or how the mechanism differs meaningfully from a small mixture-of-experts module conditioned on metadata.

The Fourier attention formulation (Eq. 3) is confusingly specified — dimensions/roles of q_f, K_f, A_i, B_i, and the global module are not rigorously defined, and the manuscript does not clarify why frequency-domain distributional differences (largely explainable by differing Nyquist/sampling rates) require a dedicated attention mechanism rather than simpler normalization.

Baseline selection is inconsistent with the extensive related-work discussion: strong recently discussed foundation models (TimesFM, MOIRAI, Timer, TIME-MOE, TTMs) are omitted from the main forecasting/imputation comparisons even though they are directly relevant competitors trained from scratch on large corpora, weakening the evaluation's completeness.

Fair-comparison concerns: GTM uses a dynamically chosen lookback window (96–1440) while baseline numbers are cited from original papers with fixed and often much shorter lookback windows, which can materially affect forecasting/imputation performance and confounds the comparison.

Despite branding the contribution as achieving 'universal knowledge representation,' the paper explicitly excludes classification/predictive tasks, undermining the universality claim relative to competitors like UniTS that already handle both generative and predictive tasks.

No reported computational cost, parameter count, or efficiency comparison against baselines, despite adding multiple low-rank Fourier modules, 2D positional encodings, and a more complex masking/pre-training pipeline — the cost-benefit tradeoff of the added complexity is not analyzed.

No code, checkpoints, or clear reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and multiple tables contain formatting errors/duplicated rows (e.g., duplicated 'electricity' row in Table 5/6), undermining confidence in careful preparation of results.

Writing quality is weak throughout (grammatical errors, inconsistent notation such as 'TTME', missing baseline entries marked '-', unclear figure captions), which affects clarity and the perceived rigor of the technical exposition.

Ablations do not cleanly disentangle whether gains stem from the specific 'granularity-awareness' design versus simply adding more parameters/attention heads (the 'w/o time_gran' and 'w/o fft' variants differ in capacity as well as design), leaving the causal claim about the value of granularity-awareness insufficiently supported.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem: universal knowledge representation for multivariate time series foundation models.

The empirical observation that time series of different sampling granularities produce different amplitude/phase-frequency joint distributions is a reasonable motivating observation, supported by KDE visualizations on a large pretraining corpus.
The unified blank-infilling pretraining objective removing the need for task-specific heads is a conceptually appealing design that, if properly validated, would simplify multi-task adaptation.

Fairly extensive experimentation across three task families (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection) with ablations and pre-train vs. no-pretrain comparisons, plus qualitative visualizations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Major mismatch between motivation and evaluation: the introduction and related work extensively discuss modern time-series foundation models (Timer, UP2ME, TimesFM, MOIRAI, TTMs, Time-MoE, UniTS) and build a dedicated comparison table (Table 1) around them, yet the actual experimental tables (2-4) compare mainly against older, non-foundation, single-dataset-trained baselines (PatchTST, FEDformer, Autoformer, Informer, DLinear) plus GPT4TS/UniTS-PMT/TimesNet. Direct quantitative comparison to TimesFM, MOIRAI, Time-MoE, TTMs, or UP2ME on forecasting/imputation is largely absent, undermining the central 'foundation model' claim.

The reported improvements are often marginal or inconsistent with the strong claims in the abstract ('outperforms SOTA across all generative tasks'). E.g., in Table 2, GTM wins only 21/50 and ties/second-best in 22/50, with PatchTST winning 14/50 and second in 15/50 — a much smaller margin than the framing suggests. TTM_E is missing MAE values entirely (dashes), suggesting incomplete/cherry-picked reporting for a strong competitor.

Pretraining gains (Tables 5, 6, 8) are very small (0.5%-7.8% MSE reduction, 1.2% F1 gain for anomaly detection), which is a weak result for a paper whose core thesis is that large-scale, granularity-aware pretraining yields substantially better 'universal' representations.

The central empirical 'finding' (different granularities have different frequency-domain statistics) is largely a restatement of basic signal-processing facts (Nyquist/sampling-rate-dependent spectral content) rather than a novel or surprising discovery; the significance of this insight for representation learning is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated (e.g., no controlled experiment isolating the specific benefit of granularity-conditioned attention versus simply providing granularity as a covariate).

Methodological details are under-specified and hard to reproduce: the low-rank Fourier attention modules operate on very short patches (patch length 96), raising doubts about the meaningfullness of the extracted 'frequency knowledge'; the quintuple granularity encoding and its interaction with the query/key attention mechanism are described only cursorily; no code or pretrained model release is mentioned, hurting reproducibility.

GTM explicitly cannot handle classification tasks (Table 1 shows 'CLF ×' for GTM), which weakens the claim of being a truly 'universal' or general-purpose time series model compared to UniTS, which handles both generative and predictive tasks.
No statistical significance testing or repeated runs (variance/error bars) are reported; all results are single-run point estimates, which is concerning given the often small performance margins.

Writing and presentation quality is weak: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('An MTS', 'devided', 'Paching', 'GTP4TS', 'the the'), inconsistent notation (e.g., percentage annotations in Table 7 with two different unexplained numbers per cell), and Table 1 relies on somewhat subjective/binary categorizations that may not fairly represent baseline capabilities (e.g., excluding FEDformer/TimeMixer++, which do use frequency-domain information, from the 'trained from scratch' comparison group).

The adaptation of GLM's autoregressive blank-infilling from NLP to continuous-valued time series regression is not well justified theoretically, and no ablation isolates the benefit of blank-infilling specifically versus a simpler unified autoregressive or masked-reconstruction pretraining scheme.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting empirical observation that time series of different sampling granularities exhibit distinct amplitude/phase-frequency joint distributions, motivating the design of granularity-aware components.

Proposes a reasonably novel architectural idea (Fourier Knowledge Attention with low-rank per-granularity modules plus a global module) that combines temporal self-attention with frequency-domain knowledge in a decoder-only backbone.

Adapts the GLM-style autoregressive blank-infilling objective to multivariate time series, which is a sensible attempt to unify forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection under one pre-training/fine-tuning scheme without task-specific heads or architecture changes.

Reasonably broad experimental coverage across three generative tasks (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection) on standard benchmark datasets, with ablations isolating the frequency module and the time-granularity attention, and pretrained-vs-non-pretrained comparisons that show consistent (if modest) gains from pretraining.
weaknesses: The headline empirical 'finding' that frequency-domain statistics differ across sampling granularities is largely expected from basic Fourier/Nyquist considerations (different sampling rates cover different frequency ranges/resolutions); the paper does not clearly establish this as a non-trivial or previously unknown insight beyond visual 3D KDE plots.

The forecasting comparison (Table 2) omits several of the most relevant, more recent foundation-model competitors that are extensively discussed in the related work and Table 1 (TimesFM, MOIRAI, Timer, UP2ME, Time-MoE, TTMs), instead comparing mainly against older transformer/MLP baselines (PatchTST, FEDformer, Autoformer, Informer, DLinear) and GPT4TS/UniTS-PMT; this weakens the claim that GTM outperforms 'SOTA' foundation models.

Reported gains over the strongest baseline (PatchTST) are often marginal or mixed (e.g., PatchTST wins or ties on several traffic/electricity metrics in Table 2), yet the text claims GTM 'outperforms all the SOTA models' and 'nearly all aspects' — this overstates the actual evidence.

The pretraining ablation (Tables 5–6, 8) shows quite small improvements (roughly 0.5%–11.7% MSE reduction, 1.2% F1 gain for anomaly detection), raising questions about how much benefit the elaborate large-scale pretraining pipeline actually provides relative to its complexity.

The 'universal knowledge representation' claim is undercut by the explicit exclusion of classification tasks (predictive tasks) from evaluation, and by Table 1 itself showing GTM does not support classification (✗), unlike some baselines (UniTS) that do — so the paper does not actually demonstrate universality across the full task taxonomy it defines in the introduction.

The discrete 'quintuple' time-granularity representation and fixed set of five learnable granularity key vectors seem ad hoc and may not generalize to arbitrary/continuous sampling rates not seen during pretraining; it is unclear how new/unseen granularities are handled, and this design implicitly requires supplying dataset-level granularity metadata at inference, which is itself a form of task/data-specific customization the paper claims to avoid.

Writing and notational quality are below standard for a top-tier venue: undefined or inconsistent symbols (e.g., q vs q_f in Eq. 3), garbled table entries ('TTME' with missing values/dashes in Table 2), inconsistent duplicate rows in Tables 5/6, and generally rough prose throughout, which hampers reproducibility and clarity.

No statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for any of the experiments, making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements are robust or within noise.

Baselines in imputation and anomaly detection tasks also miss some more recent, stronger dedicated methods (e.g., SAITS for imputation, Anomaly Transformer/DCdetector/MEMTO for anomaly detection), despite these being cited in the related work section, limiting the strength of the SOTA comparison.

The paper's core architectural contribution (low-rank Fourier attention modules per granularity) is not clearly differentiated from a small mixture-of-experts design despite claims to the contrary ('Unlike the MoE architecture, our design is closer to a knowledge attention mechanism'), and the justification for why this is meaningfully different is thin.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification tasks, compared against a broad set of SOTA baselines including recent TSFMs like Time-MOE, Sundial, TimesFM, Chronos, and MOIRAI.

The motivating analysis (Figure 1) using FFT and 2D KDE to visualize amplitude/phase-frequency joint distributions across granularities provides a reasonable empirical grounding for the architectural design choice.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the frequency-domain and time-granularity-aware components, plus scaling law analysis (model size and pretraining data) and detailed computational overhead/efficiency benchmarking (latency, memory) relevant to deployment.

Reasonably comprehensive appendix with additional real-world datasets (PV, L2C), error-bar/confidence interval analysis, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies, which strengthens reproducibility and robustness claims.

The unified pretraining framework (hybrid masking + autoregressive + reconstruction with 2D positional encoding) is a sensible engineering contribution enabling task-agnostic adaptation without architectural changes across generative tasks.
weaknesses: Performance improvements over strong baselines are frequently marginal (e.g., 0.5%-7.8% MSE reduction in forecasting, sub-1% F1 gains in anomaly detection over some baselines), raising questions about the practical/statistical significance of the claimed gains, especially since error bars are only reported for GTM itself and not for competing baselines.

The five hardcoded granularity categories (day/hour/minute/second/millisecond) used for the Fourier attention keys seem somewhat ad hoc and may not generalize well to arbitrary or continuous/mixed sampling rates, and the paper does not test robustness to unseen granularities.

The novelty is largely a combination of existing techniques (RevIN, channel independence, patching, GLM-style blank infilling, Fourier-domain attention) rather than a fundamentally new method, and the claim of being 'the first generative-task-agnostic TSFM' seems overstated given that models like UniTS and UP2ME already support multiple generative/discriminative tasks with limited task-specific modification.

The ablation study only separates two architectural components (time-granularity module and frequency module) but does not ablate the individual pieces of the proposed pretraining framework (hybrid masking, 2D positional encoding, span shuffling) to justify their individual necessity.

Some baseline comparison tables have inconsistent/missing entries (e.g., TTM_E only reporting MSE, dashes for several models/datasets), and zero-shot averages in Table 5 are computed over different subsets of datasets depending on which baselines were evaluated, which could bias the reported average rankings.
The code repository link is left blank ('available at:'), limiting immediate reproducibility verification despite claims of open resources.
Writing and notation are dense and at times inconsistent (e.g., overloaded sub/superscripts in the backbone equations), which affects clarity of the technical exposition.

strengths: The paper conducts an unusually broad set of experiments spanning forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification, plus zero-shot, few-shot, scaling, ablation, and computational-efficiency studies, which if trustworthy would provide a fairly complete picture of the model.

The idea of explicitly conditioning frequency-domain processing on temporal granularity is a reasonable and underexplored angle, and the motivating KDE analysis of amplitude/phase-frequency distributions across granularities is a nice illustrative device.

The unification of masked reconstruction and autoregressive forecasting into a single blank-infilling-style objective (with 2D positional encoding and span shuffling) is a sensible attempt to avoid task-specific heads, and the paper documents the design (patching, masking schedule, causal/full attention split) in enough detail to attempt reproduction.
Efficiency/latency breakdowns (FFT/iFFT overhead, low-rank module count vs latency, parameter/memory comparison) are a welcome addition that many TSFM papers omit.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to evidence: the abstract/intro assert GTM 'consistently outperforms SOTA models' and is the 'first generative-task-agnostic' TSFM, but the actual margins over strong baselines like PatchTST are frequently tiny (e.g., ETTh1 avg MSE .404 vs .413, Weather .225 vs .225, Traffic .385 vs .390), and in the appendix comparison against Time-MOE-Base (Table 20) GTM wins only 13 vs 12 metrics overall and loses on Weather/ETTm1 for several horizons — this does not support a 'consistently outperforms' narrative.

No statistical rigor for cross-model comparisons: error bars (Table 19) are only computed for GTM itself across seeds, not paired with baseline variance, so many of the reported 'wins' over closely-matched baselines are not shown to be statistically meaningful.

Baseline numbers for forecasting/classification are largely copied from other papers ('cite their results respectively') rather than reproduced under matched pretraining data, lookback windows, or compute budgets, which confounds attribution of gains to the proposed architecture versus differences in training data/protocol.

The granularity-aware Fourier attention design is somewhat ad hoc: time granularity is hard-coded to a quintuple with only 5 fixed 'typical' key embeddings plus a global module; it is unclear how the model generalizes to irregular or non-standard granularities not represented by the 5 anchors, and no analysis addresses this generalization gap.

Novelty is largely a recombination of existing components (RevIN, PatchTST-style patching, GLM-style blank infilling/2D positional encoding, FFT-based attention reminiscent of FEDformer) with limited new theoretical justification for why this particular combination is uniquely suited to being 'task-agnostic' beyond empirical ablations.

Classification results (Table 4) are incomplete — several baselines (UniTS-SUP/PMT) are missing ('/') for multiple datasets, making the 'best count' comparison not apples-to-apples and inflating GTM's apparent lead.
Reproducibility is undermined by an empty code link ('The code and implementation details are available at:' with no URL), despite claims of open resources.

The scaling-law claims (Section 4.8, Figure 6) are based on a very narrow data range (1G–12G) and modest model sizes (3–12 layers, dim 256–768), which is far short of the scale needed to credibly claim adherence to scaling laws in the sense used for LLMs.

Presentation relies heavily on relegating most substantive results, comparisons, and even key baselines (Sundial, Time-MOE) to the appendix, while the main text emphasizes favorable aggregate statistics ('best/second-best counts') that can obscure close or mixed results shown in the full tables.
